draft.title: Social development
card: Social development is how a person builds relationships, an identity and social skills across life. It begins in infancy and continues through adulthood.
In infancy, a child forms a close bond with a carer, called attachment. This first relationship is where children begin to learn how to relate to other people.
In childhood, social skills grow through play and school. Children learn to share, take turns, cooperate and make friends.
In adolescence, peers become more important and young people work out who they are. This process is called identity formation. It involves exploring values, interests, beliefs and roles.
draft.remember: Social development moves from bonding with carers to building skills with peers to forming a personal identity.

a.q: Which example shows social development in childhood?
opts: A six-year-old learns to take turns in a group game
A baby settles when her father picks her up
A teenager explores which values matter to her
A toddler learns that a hidden toy still exists
a.why: Learning to take turns is a social skill that grows through play and school. The baby settling shows attachment, which belongs to infancy. The toy example is about thinking, not relationships.
a.clue: Look for a social skill learned through play with other children.

b.q: Jonah, 16, joins a drama club and a debating team. He tries out different groups and decides what he believes in. What is this mainly an example of?
opts: Growing closer to carers than to peers
b.why: Jonah is exploring roles, interests and values to work out who he is, which is identity formation. Joining groups can look like building social skills, but the focus on deciding who he is points to identity. Adolescence is also when peers become more important, not carers.
b.clue: Focus on what Jonah is working out about himself.

a.best: A six-year-old learns to take turns in a group game
